An NYPD officer shot and wounded a woman Friday night after she approached police with a knife during a night of violence at a Queens home, police said.
The woman, who police have not yet identified, is in stable condition, the NYPD said.
Officials say police responded to calls of a home invasion and stabbing on 149th Street at around 9:40 Friday night. When officers arrived, no one answered the door but two men came to a second-floor window. One was injured, police said, and told officers his uncle had stabbed him and was downstairs.
Eventually, a woman on the third floor, who told police she too was afraid to go downstairs, threw keys out a window, NYPD Chief of Patrol Philip Rivera said during a press briefing.
Police said they heard screaming as they entered and were climbing the stairs. They found two men and a woman struggling in a small bedroom on the third floor in a “chaotic scene.” After officers identified themselves, they ordered the three to raise their hands. The two men complied, but the woman began moving toward the officers with the knife, Rivera said.
“The female still did not comply and moved in the direction of the officers with a knife in her hand,” Rivera told reporters. “She was within several feet of the officers when an officer discharged his firearm, striking her. She fell to the ground. An officer deployed his taser, and another officer recovered the knife.”
Rivera said officers carried the woman downstairs and gave her first aid.
The woman had stab wounds, as did three men in the home, according to police. They were all taken to local hospitals but police didn’t specify their conditions.
Rivera said police don’t believe the wounded woman was responsible for the home invasion or the initial stabbing reported in the 911 calls. The people in the home knew each other, he said, but police weren’t sure how they were related.
Investigators recovered two knives at the scene. The shooting was captured on officers’ body-worn cameras and is being investigated by the NYPD’s Force Investigation Division.
The circumstances of the stabbings and what happened inside the home before officers arrived remain under investigation.
This story is based on preliminary information provided by the NYPD and may be updated.

By

A three-faction race next week could dramatically reshape Jersey City’s long-troubled school board as the city faces eye-popping tax hikes from a school system beset by shrinking state aid, low test scores and questionable spending practices.
The three slates of candidates are competing for four seats on the nine-member board. If any single slate sweeps the election, it will likely become the dominant voting bloc for a governing body that is responsible for a $1 billion budget and roughly 26,000 students in a district still settling into full independence after 33 years of state control ended in 2022.
School board elections in Jersey City have been dominated in recent years by slates of candidates backed by the local teacher’s union, the Jersey City Education Association. But the “Education Matters” slate the union backed last time has drawn intense criticism from parents, local leaders and students around the arrest of a parent who spoke at a public meeting — and concerns the incumbents are not acting as a serious check on district leadership. The union backed a different team this time: “Leadership That Listens,” which promises to more closely scrutinize school spending.
And long-simmering dissatisfaction with the union and its leadership among parents and city leaders has given rise to an outsider slate called “For Stronger Schools.” It includes outspoken community advocates and a former board member. The group has garnered support from progressives in Jersey City who are becoming an increasingly influential voting bloc in local elections. Members of For Stronger Schools say they'll push for accountability in a district that made criminal referrals over its special education program, and just approved a five-year contract that makes its superintendent the highest-paid in the state.
There are three seats open on the board this year with full, three-year terms. There’s also a race for a one-year term seat to fill the vacancy left by former board member Matt Schneider’s resignation earlier this year.
The incumbents: Education Matters
The three incumbents seeking re-election this year — board Vice President Dejon Morris and members Alpa Patel and George Blount — are running on the Education Matters slate. They’re joined by Vanessa Rodriguez, who is seeking the one-year term.
Morris, Patel and Blount are each finishing their first terms after having been elected in 2023. Morris has become an influential member of the board, serving as its president in his first year and continuing as vice president since. This year the board approved a $1.1 billion budget that included a roughly 14% tax hike, and extended Superintendent Norma Fernandez’s contract, which made her the highest paid superintendent in the state.
Morris said re-electing the incumbents would ensure continuity in district operations and continue its momentum. He touted the district’s ban on cellphones in class, which the board approved a year before New Jersey law created a statewide ban, and facility upgrades in school buildings as major accomplishments during his first term.
But Morris has also been among the most polarizing leaders of the board since the district came out from under state control.
Ron Greco, president of the Jersey City Education Association, said the union dropped its support of Morris and the incumbent slate over issues including bickering among board members, and meetings he likened to “a kangaroo court.” He cited Morris’ behavior in particular as “disgraceful.”
Greco said the final straw for the union came in May, when Emily Pecot, the mother of a special needs student, was arrested at a board meeting. Pecot had spoken out against the board’s treatment of parents, but reportedly followed the public comment time limit. Body camera footage obtained first by Hudson County View shows Pecot later sitting quietly in the audience as police and district staff ask her to leave. Morris is heard saying that Pecot could be charged if she refused to leave. Pecot was handcuffed, arrested and charged with defiant trespass, but the charges against her were later dropped.
Morris defended his conduct at meetings: “ We were basically trying to make sure that the crowd understood that while you're allowed to voice your opinion based on your freedom of speech constitutional right, that we also have rules and regulations on how a meeting is conducted.”
If he is re-elected, Morris said his top priority would be working with city leaders and the Hudson County delegation in the State House to secure more state funding for the district.
Patel, who works in the Medicaid office of the Hudson County Department of Family Services and Reintegration, said she’s been proud of the district’s dual-enrollment program, which allows high school students to earn college credits or even associate degrees. She said she’d push to expand that program in a second term. She argued that the board during her first term navigated financial challenges while avoiding closing schools and still managing to fill important teacher and staff roles. She said she hopes voters recognize that effort.
“ Despite all these personality differences among people, the board came through very challenging times,” Patel said. “And that has to be given a big credit.”

A total of five men were arrested on trespassing and other charges in two separate manhole cases in New York City, according to police and criminal complaints revealed on Friday.
Two men who “smelled like sewage” were found on Sept. 30 on a Manhattan street corner “soaking wet,” according to a complaint. They told police they had gone into the sewer looking for jewelry.
Guenis Martinez, 33, and Wilfredo Teran Briceno, 23, were among five people arrested in two separate manhole cases in Upper Manhattan since late September.
Luis Chaparro, 28, and Jean Rosa, 31, were also arrested on the same charges in a separate case, according to police and criminal complaints.
All five people were charged with third-degree criminal trespass and trespass, both misdemeanors, according to the complaints and court records.
Martinez and Teran Briceno were arrested after the pair were caught climbing out of a manhole in Inwood. A third person, 24-year-old Xavier Guevara Lizcano, was found sitting in a nearby car waiting for them.
Four of them pleaded not guilty at their arraignments and were released without bail earlier this month, court records show. Rosa does not appear in online court records.
Lawyers for four of the men did not return messages seeking comment. An attorney for Guevara Lizcano declined to comment.
The city’s Department of Environmental Protection has warned that entering the sewers is both illegal and dangerous.
The first case began around 11 p.m. on Sept. 29, when a 911 call brought officers to Nagle Avenue in Inwood, police said.
An officer found Guevara Lizcano in the driver’s seat of a black Nissan Rogue, which he said was his, parked about a foot from a manhole cover, according to the complaint. Police found a crowbar and a screwdriver in the trunk.
Guevara Lizcano told police two people had paid him $200 that night to drive them to manholes where they could look for jewelry, the complaint says.
Later that night, a detective saw two people pop their heads out of a manhole on Nagle Avenue, then lower the cover and go back down. About 20 minutes later, a sergeant found Martinez and Teran Briceno at Broadway and Dyckman Street, the complaint says.
All three are due back in court Nov. 18, court records show.
In a separate case, shortly after midnight on Oct. 4, a police lieutenant saw two men standing over a manhole at Indian Road and West 218th Street while a third person climbed in and put the cover back over the opening, according to a second complaint.
Rosa and Chaparro were arrested at the scene. Police and the complaint did not say why the men were there, or identify the third person.
Police previously arrested two Queens men after they were seen surfacing through a sewer near Park Avenue and East 61st Street.

A 6-year-old Queens girl suffered a broken leg and a cut on her head after she was hit by falling bricks in Queens while walking with her mother on Thursday, police said.
A 4-foot-by-3-foot section of brick came loose from the side of a single-story garage on Maspeth Avenue near 59th Street on and fell to the sidewalk, the Department of Buildings said in a statement.
The department issued a violation to the property owner for what it called “failure to maintain the garage building.”
Efforts to reach the property owner were unsuccessful.
The girl was hit at about 7:30 p.m., according to the NYPD. Officers found her conscious and alert, with a fractured left thigh bone and a minor cut on the left side of her head.
She was taken to Bellevue Hospital in stable condition, officials said.

Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s administration is extending a decades-old moratorium on new street fairs through 2027, citing a likely increase in NYPD overtime.
The rule, published Friday on the City Record, will let the city reject applications for any street fair that did not take place in 2026. Fairs held this year remain eligible to renew permits next year.
The moratorium dates back to the years following 9/11, when the city stopped approving new festivals, citing the strain on the NYPD. The policy has continued every year since 2004.
The notice says the city “issues permits to over 200 street fairs and over 5,000 other events.” Issuing additional permits would drive up NYPD overtime and pull officers away from “core crime fighting, public safety and counter-terrorism duties,” the notice states.
The city comptroller projects overtime for NYPD officers will reach about $890 million in fiscal year 2026, the third-highest total on record, behind fiscal years 2024 and 2025. Police overtime for planned events, which includes parades and street fairs, rose from $97.1 million in fiscal year 2023 to $115.7 million in fiscal year 2025, according to the same report.
Open Plans, a transportation advocacy group, said the city only spent $29.5 million on uniformed overtime for street fairs and parades, which “is a drop in the bucket” in the total budget.
“An extension of the moratorium on street fairs is simply unnecessary, and the initial rationale for the ban does not hold water,” Michael Sutherland, an analyst at Open Plans, said in reaction to this year’s extension.
Michael Hyatt, president of Meteor Festivals, which produces more than a dozen street festivals in New York, said there are many non-profits, such as merchant associations and business improvement districts, that are eager to organize street fairs but can't due to the long-standing moratorium.
Other critics point to how the moratorium harms businesses in neighborhoods without a tradition of street fairs.
“Neighborhoods that have changed enormously since then have no path to a fair of their own, and a new generation of small businesses and community groups is shut out while other corridors are saturated,” said Jessica Walker, president and CEO of the Manhattan Chamber of Commerce.
Walker proposed that the administration should map where fairs cluster and where they are missing, and create a plan for including every neighborhood in the festivities.
An online hearing will be held on the moratorium on Nov. 24 at 10 a.m. before it becomes official, and Mamdani spokesperson Dora Pekec encouraged New Yorkers to participate.
"Agencies all across city government work hard to support thousands of public events every single year, bringing New Yorkers together for fairs and festivals on city streets," Pekec said in a statement. "This upcoming hearing will give New Yorkers an opportunity to once again weigh in on these longstanding rules and help us determine the best way to bring these vibrant community events to life for everyone to enjoy."

Port Authority officials on Friday touted progress on a deck over a section of the Lincoln Tunnel entrance in Hell’s Kitchen that will be a key piece of the Midtown Bus Terminal's $11 billion rebuild.
The structure covers the spaghetti-like array of approach roads that run south of West 39th Street between Dyer and Ninth avenues. It’s set to be a storage area for buses while the existing terminal is demolished and rebuilt. But after the construction project wraps, the deck will be converted into a 3.5 acre public park.
The decision to add greenspace to the neighborhood was in large part prompted by demands from local community boards to improve living conditions around the terminal, said Steve Plate, the Port Authority's chief of major capital projects, who’s overseeing the rebuild. The facility, which is used by as many as 600 buses per hour, is among the busiest bus terminals in the world.
“If you look at what green space the [neighborhood had], it’s relatively limited,” Plate said. “This was a game-changer for them and they were very thrilled about it.”
The Port Authority's bus terminal rebuild will up end an entire stretch of Hell's Kitchen for the next decade.
Courtesy Port Authority
Plate said that the underlying infrastructure of the “deckover” space is three-quarters complete and will be done by the middle of next year.
The new park and terminal project are expected to wrap up in 2035.
During a tour of the construction site, Port Authority Executive Director Kathryn Garcia explained the agency is essentially building a bridge over the roadways that carry car traffic in and out of the Lincoln Tunnel.
The agency is propping up the deck with massive steel columns that weigh between 30 to 40 tons. Once the structure is complete, workers will pour concrete over the new deck.
Building the future park space is one of the first steps in a major construction effort, which is bound to cause disruptions for bus commuters in the region. Garcia said the bulk of the disruptions will occur in the project's early phase as the Port Authority reroutes buses entering and exiting the terminal.
Ramsey Khalifeh / Gothamist
The agency has deconstructed some of the bus terminal’s existing elevated ramps to make way for new ramp structures. Starting last week, buses entering the terminal on non-express bus lane buses during afternoon service began to be rerouted around to West 39th Street to access another ramp to get to the terminal’s gates.
A backlog of buses were waiting in a line to use the alternative ramp during the Port Authority’s tour of the construction site Friday. One bus driver was unable to make the sharp turn onto the ramp and had to back up, which held up traffic.
Garcia said any travel hiccups caused by the construction will be worthwhile because bus riders will get a shiny new station.
“We are doing this because we know that we can deliver an amazing experience … This is what we plan to bring when we finish completion of this $11 billion project, both functional and efficient, but also beautiful. We can do two things at the same time,” Garcia said. “It’ll be a real welcoming gateway.”

Black couple seeking Queens apartment sues over racist text from broker

A couple who mistakenly received a racist text message at an apartment viewing this summer is now suing the real estate company, the broker and the landlord for discrimination.
According to the lawsuit filed in state court this week, Lisa Renee Olaso and Cyril Christopher were scheduled to view a three-bedroom unit in a home on 26th Avenue in Flushing in June.
But when they arrived and prepared to get out of their car to see the apartment, they got a text that the broker Helen Tzelios apparently meant to send to just the landlord: “Ugh, they’re Black.”
Tzelios, who worked for Douglas Elliman Realty, had never met the couple in person before, according to the couple's lawyer Kenneth Mollins. When a tearful Olaso asked her about the message, Tzelios allegedly said it was referring to other Black people who had “caused problems” in the neighborhood before.
Olaso said she was shocked by the text and initially doubted whether she had read it correctly. Then, reality set in.
"You saw exactly what you saw. You got a text that was meant to go to someone else," she told Gothamist in an interview.
Olaso said she decided to file the lawsuit to showcase how racism exists today.
"And these are people, all races, just many of us who are just working class, good people, we're just sick of ignorant things that other people do to make everybody else look bad," she said.
Olaso and Christopher were “upset and humiliated” and declined to see the apartment after that exchange, according to the suit, which also alleges that the message violated the federal Fair Housing Act.
Mollins said the couple was unsure what to do, but finally decided to take legal action to show that racism and discrimination still exist in New York.
Just 3% of residents of Queens Community District 7 — which includes Flushing, Murray Hill, and Whitestone — identify as Black, according to 2024 census data.
As housing becomes increasingly scarce, it’s easier for landlords to discriminate and harder for tenants to challenge it, according to Where We Live NYC — the city’s fair housing planning initiative.
“ Racism isn't always someone wearing a white hood. Sometimes it's someone holding the keys to a house, and they won't allow Black families to belong there,” Mollins said.
He said the experience was especially shocking to Olaso and Christopher because it was one of their first tastes of New York City. They were looking to move to the five boroughs from Delaware.
“ They felt it was a culturally diverse area that's not going to have that type of discrimination,” he said.
A spokesperson for Douglas Elliman said the company has a zero-tolerance policy for discrimination and that Tzelios was fired. Tzelios did not immediately answer a text message.
Charles and Barbara Neocleous, who are listed online and in the lawsuit as the landlords of the apartment in question, did not answer a phone call and did not respond to a voicemail.
Mollins said the couple is not suing for money.
Olaso works as an airline manager and Christopher works as a surgical technician at a hospital in Brooklyn, Mollins said. They ended up finding a place to rent in Commack, on Long Island.
For Olaso, the decision to speak up about what happened was to honor Black Americans who fought for their civil rights in the past.
"The reason why many of us have the opportunities that we have is because people before us fought. They fought for change. They fought for opportunity. They walked. Some of them sacrificed their lives for us," she said.
Sweeping racism under the rug would do nothing for progress, especially for her son, as well as her nieces and nephews, she said.
"How am I going to make change if I just sweep things under the rug? And this is not easy, but I feel like it wasn't easy for people back in the day, but sometimes we have to stand for change," Olaso said.

The midterm elections are finally here. Early in-person voting in New Jersey kicks off on Saturday, Oct. 24 and runs until Nov. 1.
Vote-by-mail has been open for several weeks and remains an option for Garden State voters until Election Day, Nov. 3.
For those waiting until the big day, polls across the state will be open from 6 a.m. to 8 p.m.
Election results in at least one New Jersey race could help determine whether Democrats or Republicans will hold the majority in the House and Senate for the remainder of President Donald Trump’s term.
Here are the key races we’re keeping an eye on in New Jersey:
The Big One
Kean vs. Bennett in New Jersey’s 7th Congressional District is the state’s marquee race this year.
Rep. Tom Kean Jr., the two-term Republican incumbent, is the scion of one of the Garden State’s most well-known political families. His father served two terms as a popular governor in the 1980s. Kean himself served in the state Legislature for two decades. He won his district easily in the past two elections.
Kean’s challenger is first-time Democratic nominee Rebecca Bennett. She’s a millennial mom, a former Navy helicopter pilot with 15 years of military experience, and a healthcare executive. Her background as a pilot and her center-left stance on key issues like healthcare and immigration have drawn comparisons between Bennett and the state’s Democratic Gov. Mikie Sherrill.
Democrat Rebecca Bennett campaigning in Bernards Township, New Jersey.
Aristide Economopoulos for Gothamist
Republicans enjoy about a 19,000-voter advantage in the district, which stretches from the eastern edge of Central Jersey across the state to the Pennsylvania border. But pollsters and political watchdogs have called the race a toss-up that could lean Democratic.
Kean was absent from Congress for 116 days earlier this year and missed over 100 votes while being treated for depression. Since returning to the campaign trail at the end of June, Kean has tried to cast Bennett as too liberal for the conservative-leaning district. At the same time, he’s had to contend with Trump’s slumping popularity numbers in New Jersey.
Republican Rep. Tom Kean, Jr. in Washington D.C.
Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images
To woo Republicans and Independents, Bennett has focused her campaign less on cultural issues and more on affordability, like reducing the costs of healthcare and childcare.
But controversy surrounding a proposed ICE facility in the district, Kean’s absence from Congress and his stock trading while in office have also been discussion points throughout the campaign.
The ‘magnitude’ of a win
Other congressional races across the state are less competitive, but margins of victory and voter turnout in other districts should reveal strengths and weaknesses in the candidates and their parties.
In South Jersey, Republican Rep. Jeff Van Drew is running against Democrat Zack Mullock in New Jersey’s 2nd Congressional District.
Democrats around the state have mused about taking out Van Drew ever since Sherrill flipped several red counties in his district blue during the 2025 gubernatorial. The Cook Political Report has this race ranked “solid R” in the GOP’s favor. But Matt Hale, a politics professor at Seton Hall University, said the two-term Republican could be at risk if Democrats outperform expectations and turn a blue wave into a “tsunami.”
“If that happens, the magnitude of the [Democratic] tsunami nationwide will be something like we've never seen,” he said.
Democratic Rep. Analilia Mejia
Analilia Mejia for New Jersey
In North Jersey, far-left progressive Democratic Rep. Analilia Mejia is running for her first full term in Congress. She’s facing Republican Joe Hathaway, whom she beat by 21 points in April’s special election. The district spans six counties and includes a mix of urban and suburban towns, including liberal strongholds like Maplewood and Montclair.
Mejia is heavily favored to beat Hathaway again. Political analysis sites Cook Political Report and Decision Desk HQ rate the race “ safe” for Democrats. Another progressive, first-time candidate Dr. Adam Hamawy is also expected to win in the state’s heavily Democratic 12th District near Trenton.
But for New Jersey Democrats, the real test will be the margins of victory. Strong turnout could signal whether the party’s progressive movement has enduring strength.
In New Jersey’s 9th District, Democratic Rep. Nellie Pou is running against Rosie Pino, a Republican town councilmember from Clifton.
The district includes much of Passaic County, where nearly 50% of the population is Latino. Trump unexpectedly carried Passaic County in the 2024 presidential election thanks to impressive turnout among Latino voters. But Pou also outperformed her party that year, beating Republican Billy Prempeh by roughly 5 points.
Democrats have said they hope Pou's strong victory this year indicates that a large chunk of Latino voters have returned to their party, at least for now.
Cory Booker’s time to shine?
With no presidential race this year, Sen. Cory Booker gets the privilege of sitting at the top of the Democrats' ballot.
Booker is seeking his fourth statewide victory since winning a 2013 special election after Sen. Frank Lautenberg's death.
